claims.text: At 600–800 °C, the wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed by formation of a stable, adherent oxide layer.
The oxide layer acts as a self-healing wear barrier.
Coatings possessing the oxide layer will lose less material than coatings lacking it.
The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating has a nano- to micro-crystalline grain structure.
The as-deposited coating has no pre-existing oxide film.
High-temperature exposure in air, relative to treatment at the same temperature in an inert atmosphere, will produce a nanostructured oxide film at the coating surface and along grain boundaries.
High temperature promotes oxidation at selective sites in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
A continuous or semi-continuous oxide film reduces friction.
A continuous or semi-continuous oxide film impedes microscale material removal.
The oxide film heals minor abrasions during wear.
Air-treated coatings will exhibit significantly lower wear rates than inert-treated coatings.
Air-treated coatings will exhibit lower friction coefficients than inert-treated coatings.
Air-treated coatings will exhibit a more uniform wear pattern than inert-treated coatings.
SEM/EDS or XPS will reveal a continuous, adherent oxide layer on the air-treated coating that is less apparent or absent on the inert-treated coating.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply during cyclic wear at 600–800 °C under loading typical of high-temperature protective-coating applications.
The mechanism may not apply at substantially different oxidation potentials or at temperatures insufficient to form the oxide layer.
A lack of significantly reduced wear rate and friction in the air-treated coating relative to the inert-treated control would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe a continuous, adherent oxide film associated with improved wear resistance would falsify the proposed oxide-mediated mechanism.
